---
title: "Channels"
guide-section: "Guide"
---

A channel is a two-way message link between a Python process and a helper
process that it spawns: one lock-free ring per direction, over shared memory.
One process writes data and the other reads it in place — never copied
through a socket, pipe, or file.

## Creating a channel

`Channel.create()` spawns the peer process (`python -m pymizu.child <token>`)
and connects both ends.
The peer program is a Python source string, evaluated in the peer with `ch`
bound to its side of the channel:

```{python}
import pymizu

ch = pymizu.Channel.create("""
import pymizu
while True:
    x = ch.recv()
    if x is pymizu.CLOSED:
        break
    ch.send(x)
""")
```

The peer is a full Python process: it imports anything importable in the
spawning interpreter's environment.
`Channel.create()` returns once the peer has attached (up to
`startup_timeout` seconds, raising `StartupError` otherwise).

A `launcher` changes how the peer is spawned — it is one callable that takes
the join token and arranges for a Python process to run
`python -m pymizu.child <token>`.
`pymizu.r_launcher()` is the built-in example: it spawns an R peer instead
(see [R interop](interop.qmd)).
`Channel.attach(token)` is the low-level peer-side entry; user code spawns
peers through a launcher.

## Sending and receiving

`ch.send()` publishes a payload, visible to the peer the moment the call
returns.
Sends never block for ring space.
`ch.recv()` returns the next payload, waiting up to `timeout` seconds
(indefinitely when omitted):

```{python}
ch.send([1, "a", None])
ch.recv(timeout=5)
```

Outcomes that end a conversation — ring full, timeout, orderly close, peer
death — come back as sentinel singletons, never raised:

| Sentinel | Returned when |
|---|---|
| `pymizu.FULL` | a send finds the ring full |
| `pymizu.TIMEOUT` | a receive's timeout expires |
| `pymizu.CLOSED` | the peer has closed and the ring is drained |
| `pymizu.PEER_GONE` | the peer process has died and the ring is drained |

Test them by identity — `x is pymizu.TIMEOUT` — or with
`pymizu.is_sentinel(x)`.
No call needs an error handler.
If the peer dies, receives first drain what it already published, then report
`PEER_GONE`.

`send_batch()` and `recv_batch()` move several payloads in one crossing — use
them at rates where per-call overhead starts to matter:

```{python}
ch.send_batch(range(4))
ch.recv_batch(4, timeout=5)
```

`ch.alive()` reports whether the peer still runs, without touching the rings.
`ch.info()` returns a read-only wire-state snapshot.

## Closing

`ch.close()` is the orderly shutdown: it signals the peer and waits for it to
finish draining before releasing the shared resources:

```{python}
ch.close()
```

A channel is also a context manager — the `with` block closes it on exit.
`close_signal()` signals without waiting; `destroy()` tears the handle down
immediately and the peer sees `PEER_GONE`.

## What crosses a channel

The staging path picks the first tier that matches:

1. `None` crosses as an immediate — no bytes move.
2. Buffer-protocol objects (`bytes`, 1-D contiguous numpy arrays) ride a
   serialization-free raw tier: float64, int32, int64, complex128, and uint8
   cross unchanged, arriving as arrays (`bytes` arrives as uint8).
   A large buffer crosses as a zero-copy read-only view over the shared
   pages — no copy, no parse.
3. A `str` within the inline budget crosses as raw UTF-8.
4. Booleans, numbers, and flat containers of them ride a compact binary
   codec.
5. Everything else crosses as a pickle protocol 4 stream.

Every handle knows its peer's language (a per-region identity exchange at
handshake).
On a Python-to-Python channel that is the whole story: identity dtypes ride
the raw tier, everything else pickles unchanged.
On a foreign-language channel (an R peer), staging switches to the `'I'`
interchange stream: a portable subset crosses, and a value outside it raises
`pymizu.DeclinedError` at send time, naming the value's path and the reason —
the channel is unharmed.
See [R interop](interop.qmd).

An uncaught error in the peer crosses as a value, not a raised exception: a
`pymizu.TaskError` carrying the original exception's class name and traceback
text.
`pymizu.is_remote_error(x)` tests a received value; raise it to propagate.

## Sizing

`Channel.create()` takes `capacity` (ring slots, a power of two),
`slot_size` (bytes per slot — the inline payload budget is
`slot_size - 16`), and `arena_size` (the channel's spill arena).
A payload past the inline budget spills to the arena or a fresh
shared-memory region.
`spin=True` selects pure-spin waiting: receivers never park to the OS — the
lowest-latency mode, at full CPU use while waiting.
